q8.answer: Session state lives in Postgres, in the `sessions` table, keyed by the SHA-256 hex of the session ID. Either app instance reads the row from the shared database, so no instance holds session state in memory and the load balancer needs no sticky sessions.

q9.answer: Each email's failures are kept in the `login_throttle` table, keyed by the trimmed lowercase email, in a `failed_at` timestamp array. On each checked failure the app takes the database clock time, appends it, drops entries older than 10 minutes, and counts what remains including the current attempt; a count of 5 sets a 15-minute `locked_until` and clears the list.

q10.answer: The server hashes the cookie value and runs one UPDATE on `sessions` joined to `users`, matching `id_hash`, `last_seen_at` later than now minus 30 minutes, and `expires_at` later than now. When it matches, it writes back `last_seen_at = now()` and returns the user's id and email, so the 30-minute idle clock restarts on every accepted request.

q11.answer: The whole login transaction rolls back, so no session row, throttle change or attempt count is kept, and the browser gets a 503 page saying sign-in is temporarily unavailable, with no Set-Cookie. A cookie is sent only after COMMIT succeeds.

q12.answer: A sweep job, run by a 10-minute timer on each instance and guarded by pg_try_advisory_xact_lock so only one run does the work, deletes session rows whose `expires_at` has passed or whose `last_seen_at` is more than 30 minutes old. Logout and login rotation also delete rows directly, and the sweep never removes a session the protected-request check would accept.
